output.brief: The evidence points mainly to the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office. Applications and admits rose and admitted GPA edged up, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield fell sharply only in the tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's from 45.2% to 31.9% and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential (award unchanged) and no-award admits stayed roughly flat, so this is not a general softening in demand. Early-action admits had no processing delay and their yield still fell about as much as regular decision (7.4 vs 7.5 points). That makes slow turnaround an unlikely main driver, though it may have cost individual students like the one in the counsellor's email. I could not tell whether the portal lost documents; no direct evidence exists. I'm fairly confident, though the tier data is not split by round and the award cut was not isolated from other factors. Next steps: do not replace the director on this basis. Take the award schedule back to the finance committee with a modelled revenue trade-off for the tiers that lost yield, before award letters go out. Also set a monthly-reported turnaround target, and check the transcript issue before ordering any vendor rebuild.
